lead: A continuous-wave (CW) radar transmits all the time and never times a pulse. It listens for the small frequency shift that a moving target puts on the echo, the Doppler shift, and so it measures speed only. If the transmit frequency is swept in a straight line, the echo returns with a delay, and mixing echo with transmitter gives a beat frequency proportional to range. That is frequency-modulated CW (FMCW) radar, used in aircraft radio altimeters, tank level gauges and car radar; the plain CW radar is the police speed gun.
prereq: You need R = c t / 2 from Radar principle, block diagram and frequency bands and the idea of a mixer from RF circuits and transceivers.

sections.h3: The Doppler shift and the CW radar

blocks.text: The echo from a target at range R has travelled 2R, so its phase lags the transmitter by φ = 2π(2R/λ) = 4πR/λ radians. If the target moves, R changes and the phase turns; a turning phase is a frequency. With radial velocity v<sub>r</sub> = −dR/dt (positive when the target closes):

fd = 2 vr / λ = 2 vr f0 / c
Here fd is the Doppler shift in Hz; vr is the radial velocity in m/s, the part of the target velocity along the line of sight (v cos θ for a target moving at angle θ to that line); λ = c/f0 is the wavelength in m.
A closing target raises the echo frequency; an opening target lowers it. A target crossing the beam at right angles has v<sub>r</sub> = 0 and gives no shift at all.

A CW radar has one oscillator at f<sub>0</sub> running continuously. Because the transmitter never stops, it usually has separate transmit and receive antennas, so the strong transmit signal does not swamp the receiver. A mixer multiplies the echo by a sample of the transmitter; a filter keeps the difference frequency f<sub>d</sub>, and a counter or FFT reads it. Better sets mix down to an intermediate frequency first, avoiding the flicker noise of the mixer at low frequencies, and use I and Q outputs to tell closing from opening targets.
A CW radar cannot measure range: the wave has no timing mark. It also ignores anything stationary (f<sub>d</sub> = 0), and two cars at the same speed at different distances give one tone.

sections.h3: FMCW radar: a sweep gives range

blocks.text: An FMCW radar sweeps its frequency linearly by Δf over a time T<sub>m</sub>. The echo from range R returns after t = 2R/c, by which time the transmitter has moved on by Δf·t/T<sub>m</sub>. Mixing echo with transmitter gives that difference, the beat frequency:

blocks.where: f<sub>b</sub> is the beat frequency in Hz; R the range in m; Δf the sweep width in Hz; T<sub>m</sub> the duration of one sweep in s.

blocks.text: For a triangular sweep with modulation frequency f<sub>m</sub> (one up-sweep and one down-sweep each period), each sweep lasts T<sub>m</sub> = 1/(2f<sub>m</sub>) and the formula becomes f<sub>b</sub> = 4RΔf·f<sub>m</sub>/c, the form many textbooks print. The range resolution depends only on the sweep width:

blocks.where: ΔR is the range resolution in m. A 150 MHz sweep resolves 1 m.

blocks.text: A moving target adds its Doppler shift to the beat. On the up-sweep the two subtract, on the down-sweep they add (for a closing target), so the triangular sweep separates them:

fR = (fup + fdown) / 2
Here fR is the range part of the beat; fup = fR − fd and fdown = fR + fd are the measured beats, so fd = (fdown − fup)/2.
The figure draws both sweeps and both beats for the second worked example.

sections.h3: Multiple-frequency CW and where each is used

blocks.text: Range can also come from two CW tones f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub>. Each echo lags by 4πR/λ, so the phase difference between the two echoes is Δφ = 4πRΔf/c, with Δf = f<sub>2</sub> − f<sub>1</sub>. Measuring Δφ gives R, unambiguously while Δφ stays below 2π, that is up to R = c/(2Δf): 1 MHz spacing gives 150 m. Not every syllabus covers this multiple-frequency method; it is used in survey instruments.

head: Property
CW
FMCW
rows: radio altimeter, level gauge, car radar

blocks.text: A police speed gun is CW: it needs only f<sub>d</sub>. A radio altimeter is FMCW, sweeping around 4.3 GHz and reading the beat from the ground. A tank level gauge is FMCW, because it must report the distance to the liquid surface, which hardly moves. Car radars at 77 GHz are FMCW with fast sweeps and several receive antennas, so they read range, speed and angle together.

examples.question: (a) A police CW radar works at 10.525 GHz and a car approaches head-on at 100 km/h. Find λ and f<sub>d</sub>. (b) An FMCW radio altimeter sweeps Δf = 100 MHz in T<sub>m</sub> = 1 ms. Find the beat frequency for ground 150 m below.
steps: v<sub>r</sub> = 100/3.6 = 27.78 m/s, positive because the car closes.
examples.answer: λ = 2.85 cm and f<sub>d</sub> = 1949 Hz (about 19.5 Hz per km/h); the altimeter beat is 100 kHz.

examples.question: A 77 GHz car radar uses a triangular sweep of Δf = 150 MHz with each up- and down-sweep lasting T<sub>m</sub> = 1 ms. It measures f<sub>up</sub> = 49.73 kHz and f<sub>down</sub> = 70.27 kHz from a car ahead. Find the range, the closing speed and the range resolution.
steps: Range part: f<sub>R</sub> = (49.73 + 70.27)/2 = 60.00 kHz. Doppler part: f<sub>d</sub> = (70.27 − 49.73)/2 = 10.27 kHz.
v<sub>r</sub> = f<sub>d</sub>λ/2 = 10 270 × 3.896 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 20.0 m/s (72 km/h), closing because the down-sweep beat is the higher one.
examples.answer: The car is 60.0 m ahead and closing at 20.0 m/s (72 km/h); the radar resolves 1.0 m in range.

traps: Writing f<sub>d</sub> = v<sub>r</sub>/λ. The wave is shifted on the way out and again on the way back, so it is 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ.
Putting km/h into 2v/λ. Convert first: 100 km/h is 27.78 m/s.
Using the full speed of a car that is not coming straight at the radar. Only v cos θ counts; a car crossing the beam gives no shift.
Using the carrier f<sub>0</sub> in the FMCW range formula. The beat comes from the sweep width Δf; f<sub>0</sub> enters only through the Doppler term.
Saying a CW radar measures range, or sees a stationary target. A single-frequency CW radar does neither.

quiz.q: State the Doppler formula for a monostatic radar and the sign convention for v<sub>r</sub>.
quiz.a: f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ, with v<sub>r</sub> positive for a closing target, which raises the echo frequency.

quiz.q: Why can a single-frequency CW radar measure speed but not range?
quiz.a: The transmitted wave has no timing mark, so the delay cannot be measured; only the frequency difference f<sub>d</sub>, which gives radial speed, is available.

quiz.q: A CW radar at 5.8 GHz sees a car moving away at 54 km/h. Find the Doppler shift with its sign.
An FMCW radar has Δf = 200 MHz and T<sub>m</sub> = 2 ms. Find f<sub>b</sub> for R = 60 m and the range resolution.
A 10 GHz CW radar watches two cars approaching at 60 km/h, one at 20 m and one at 60 m. What does it show, and what change would separate them?
quiz.a: Both give the same f<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 16.67 / 0.03 = 1111 Hz, one spectral line, with no range. An FMCW sweep (or a pulse radar) adds range, so the two appear at different beat frequencies.

quiz.q: Why does a CW radar usually have separate transmit and receive antennas?
quiz.a: The transmitter is on all the time, so its leakage into the receiver would mask or overload the weak echo. Separate antennas give isolation; one antenna would need a circulator, which still leaks.

quiz.q: How does a triangular sweep separate range from Doppler in FMCW radar?
quiz.a: For a closing target the up-sweep beat is f<sub>R</sub> − f<sub>d</sub> and the down-sweep beat f<sub>R</sub> + f<sub>d</sub>. Their average gives f<sub>R</sub>, hence range; half their difference gives f<sub>d</sub>, hence speed, and which beat is larger gives the direction.

beyond: Car radars at 76–81 GHz sweep in tens of microseconds and send many sweeps per frame. A fast Fourier transform within each sweep gives range, a second one across the sweeps gives speed, and several receive antennas add angle (MIMO radar). The same FMCW principle measures the thickness of ice sheets from aircraft. Search for "range-Doppler FFT" and "FMCW MIMO radar" to go further.

figure.caption: Top: the transmitted triangle sweeps 150 MHz up in 1 ms and back down; the echo returns late (enlarged here) and shifted by the Doppler. Bottom, to scale: the beat is 49.73 kHz on the up-sweep and 70.27 kHz on the down-sweep; their mean, 60 kHz, gives 60 m and half their gap, 10.27 kHz, gives 20 m/s.
